The pairs (p,q) such that the Hodge number h^{pq} of \operatorname {H}^n(X) are non-zero satisfy the following conditions:
(p,q)\in [0,n]\times [0,n].
If \dim X=N, and n\geqslant N, then (p,q)\in [n-N,N]\times [n-N,N].
If X is proper, then p+q\leqslant n.
If X is smooth, then p+q\geqslant n. The same conclusion holds if X is an equidimensional "rational homology manifold" of dimension N, i.e. if, for all x\in X, \operatorname {H}^i_{(x)}(X,\mathbb {Q}) = \begin {cases} 0 &\text {if }i\neq 2N \\\mathbb {Q} &\text {if }i=2N. \end {cases}

Let Y \xrightarrow {f} X \overset {j}{\hookrightarrow } \overline {X} be morphisms of schemes. Suppose that Y is proper and X is smooth, and that \overline {X} is a smooth compactification of X. Then \operatorname {H}^\bullet (\widetilde {X},\mathbb {Q}) and \operatorname {H}^\bullet (X,\mathbb {Q}) have the same image in \operatorname {H}^\bullet (Y,\mathbb {Q}).

The proof is parallel to that of . It suffices to prove, for any i and any n, that \operatorname {Gr}_i^W(f^*) and \operatorname {Gr}_i^W((jf)^*) have the same image in \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q}).
For i>n, these images are both zero since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iii) of ).
For i<n, these images are both zero since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(X,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iv) of ).
For i=n, these images are equal since \operatorname {Gr}_n^W(j^*) is surjective ().

Let \widetilde {X} \xrightarrow {\pi } X \xrightarrow {f} Y be morphisms of schemes. Suppose that Y is smooth, X is proper, \widetilde {X} is smooth and proper, and that \pi is surjective. Then the kernels of f^* and (f\pi )^* in \operatorname {H}^\bullet (Y,\mathbb {Q}) are equal.

We will prove that \operatorname {Ker}(\operatorname {Gr}_i^W(f^*))=\operatorname {Ker}(\operatorname {Gr}_i^W((f\pi )^*)) in \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q}).
For i<n, these kernels are both zero since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iv) of ).
For i>n, these kernels are both all of \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q}) since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(X,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iii) of ).
For i=n, these kernels are equal since \operatorname {Gr}_n^W(\pi ^*) is injective ().

This article follows Hodge Theory I and Hodge Theory II; the numbering of the sections here follows that of (which contains to ).

In , we introduced the Hodge theory of non-singular (not necessarily complete) algebraic varieties. Here we treat the case of arbitrary singularities. From onwards, we will make essential use of results from to .

In the case of an arbitrary algebraic variety X, we "replace" X by a smooth simplicial scheme X_\bullet with compactification given by a smooth projective simplicial scheme \overline {X}_\bullet . We can further arrange things so that \overline {X}_n\setminus X_n is a normal crossing divisor, given by a union of smooth divisors D_{n,i}. We thus "express", via a spectral sequence, the cohomology of X in terms of the cohomology of the p-fold intersections of the D_{n,i} (for n,p\geqslant 0), and we obtain an induced mixed Hodge structure on H^\bullet (X).

In , we define the mixed Hodge structure of \operatorname {H}^n(X,\mathbb {Z}) (for X a separated scheme). We show that the Hodge numbers h^{pq} of \operatorname {H}^n(X,\mathbb {Z}) can only be non-zero for (p,q)\in [0,n]\times [0,n]. For n>\dim X, we have a more precise result (). If X is smooth (resp. complete), they can only be non-zero if, further, p+q\geqslant n (resp. p+q\leqslant n). If X is a complete subscheme of Z, with complement U, with Z complete and smooth of dimension n, then we can, by N. Katz, interpret this "duality" between the complete case and the smooth case as coming from the "Alexander duality" \to \ldots \to \operatorname {H}^i(Z,\mathbb {Q}) \to \operatorname {H}^i(X,\mathbb {Q}) \to (\operatorname {H}^{2n-i-1}(U,\mathbb {Q}))^* \to \operatorname {H}^{i+1}(Z,\mathbb {Q}) \to \ldots .
From the functorial properties of the theory thus constructed, we obtain the useful corollaries to , which we state in terms independent of any Hodge theory.

In , we endow the cohomology of any simplicial scheme X_\bullet with a mixed Hodge structure. This generality is not illusory.
We can interpret relative cohomology spaces as being the cohomology of suitable simplicial schemes.
Let B_G be the classifying space of the underlying Lie group of an algebraic group G. We can interpret the cohomology of B_G as being the cohomology of a suitable simplicial scheme.

In , after having calculated the mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of B_G (for G linear), we thus obtain that of G. As a corollary, we find that, if a linear group G acts on a non-singular complete variety X, then the map \operatorname {H}^\bullet (X,\mathbb {Q}) \to \operatorname {H}^\bullet (X,\mathbb {Q})\otimes \operatorname {H}^\bullet (G,\mathbb {Q}) factors through \operatorname {H}^\bullet (X,\mathbb {Q})\otimes \operatorname {H}^0(G,\mathbb {Q})\subset \operatorname {H}^\bullet (X,\mathbb {Q})\otimes \operatorname {H}^\bullet (G,\mathbb {Q}).
In , we interpret in terms of abelian schemes the mixed Hodge structures of pure degree \{(-1,-1),(-1,0),(0,-1),(0,0)\} (see ), and we consider in detail the \operatorname {H}^1 of curves.

The theory developed up until here is an absolute theory (we do not study the functors \mathrm {R} f_*), and deals only with constant coefficients. I conjecture that, if \mathscr {H} is a variation of polarisable Hodge structures (in the sense of Griffiths [G1970a]) on a scheme X, then the cohomology of X with coefficients in the local system \mathscr {H} is endowed with a natural mixed Hodge structure. I can only prove this when X is complete.

Let \widetilde {X} \xrightarrow {\pi } X \xrightarrow {f} Y be morphisms of schemes. Suppose that Y is smooth, X is proper, \widetilde {X} is smooth and proper, and that \pi is surjective. Then the kernels of f^* and (f\pi )^* in \operatorname {H}^\bullet (Y,\mathbb {Q}) are equal.

We will prove that \operatorname {Ker}(\operatorname {Gr}_i^W(f^*))=\operatorname {Ker}(\operatorname {Gr}_i^W((f\pi )^*)) in \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q}).
For i<n, these kernels are both zero since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iv) of ).
For i>n, these kernels are both all of \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(Y,\mathbb {Q}) since \operatorname {Gr}_i^W\operatorname {H}^n(X,\mathbb {Q})=0 ((iii) of ).
For i=n, these kernels are equal since \operatorname {Gr}_n^W(\pi ^*) is injective ().
